manifest.name: dsh-win-control
manifest.description: DeepSeek Harness plugin for controlling a Windows desktop: program-first automation (windows, UIA, OCR, browser CDP), humanised mouse and keyboard input, live control panel. Detects the machine at first run, writes its own config and degrades gracefully where a capability is missing.

readme.text:
DeepSeek Harness plugin that drives a Windows desktop: program-first automation
(window control, UI Automation, browser CDP, local Windows OCR), humanised
mouse/keyboard input, and a live control panel.

On first activation the plugin probes the machine and writes its own config to
`<DSH_HOME>/computer-control/config.json`: Windows version, PowerShell version, screen
size, OCR engine + languages, UI Automation availability, python/pypinyin. Every later
run reuses that file (re-read every few seconds, edits are honoured), and each tool
adapts to it:

- no OCR language pack -> computer_find_text says so immediately instead of failing deep
- no python+pypinyin -> typing mode "ime" goes straight to direct Unicode typing
- no UI Automation -> computer_uia explains it; computer_act still uses OCR
- no browser on a CDP port -> computer_dom explains how to launch one
- a Harness UI without the expected slots -> the panel is skipped, Host tools keep working
- `computer_selftest` re-probes and rewrites the config on demand

readme.section: Browser pages are read, not scanned
readme.text:
- `computer_dom` speaks the Chrome DevTools Protocol directly (dependency-free WebSocket
  client): read `innerText`/`outerHTML`, run JavaScript, click a selector, navigate, or
  launch Edge/Chrome with an isolated profile and `--remote-debugging-port`.
- `computer_page_text` reads the whole page through UI Automation TextPattern, with a local
  OCR dump as fallback.
- `computer_find_text` with an empty `text` dumps every recognized line of any window.

readme.section: Browser pages are read, not scanned
readme.text:
Prefer HTTP (`web_fetch`) for public pages and the readers above for logged-in or
JS-rendered pages; OCR stays the fallback for canvas, games and self-drawn apps.

Requirements: Windows 10/11 and a DeepSeek Harness build that can install profile bundles.
Everything else ships with Windows (powershell.exe, user32/gdi32/imm32, UI Automation,
WinRT OCR).

```
dsh plugin --profile <name> add dsh-win-control
```

A DeepSeek Harness plugin that lets the agent — and you — drive this Windows desktop:
screen captures, mouse movement/clicks/scroll/drag, and keyboard text or key chords.

One implementation, two callers: every button in the on-screen panel calls the same
Host operation that the agent tools call, so the two surfaces cannot drift apart.
There are three ways to look at the screen, and only the last one touches the disk:

1. **Panel preview (you)** — a persistent PowerShell worker captures frames into memory.
   Host keeps the latest frame in memory, the panel renders it from a Blob object URL and
   revokes the previous URL as soon as the next frame arrives. Zero disk writes; a frame
   costs ~90–150 ms, so the panel refreshes at 0.5 s / 1 s / 2 s.
2. **`computer_look` (the agent)** — the frame is captured in memory, saved as a
   *transient* attachment only long enough for one model call, and that object file is
   deleted immediately after the answer. The agent receives text, never a picture, so
   nothing accumulates in the attachment library.
3. **`computer_screenshot` with `includeImage: true` or `path`** — the only explicit
   "keep it" option: the picture is attached to the conversation (Harness attachment
   library, never auto-deleted) or written to the path you name.

- **Pointer**: relative `SendInput` moves (`MOUSEEVENTF_MOVE`) along a quadratic bezier with a
  random curvature and 5–14 ms per step, instead of teleporting with `SetCursorPos`; a 60–180 ms
  settle follows before the button goes down.
- **Typing**: three real paths —
  - `typing: "ime"` converts Chinese to pinyin (via the local `python` + `pypinyin`, bundled
    `scripts/pinyin.py`), types the pinyin as virtual-key events so the input method composes
    and shows its candidate window, commits with Space, then OCR-verifies the first characters;
    if the IME was not composing it undoes (`Ctrl+Z`) and types the text directly, so the
    result is always what was asked for.
  - `typing: "keys"` sends virtual-key events only (no Chinese conversion).
  - `typing: "unicode"` injects characters directly (safe for Chinese/emoji without an IME).
  - `"auto"` (default) uses keys for ASCII-only text and unicode when the text contains non-ASCII.
  Per-character delay 20–85 ms with an occasional 80–240 ms pause.

`typing: "ime"` needs a Chinese IME in Chinese mode (press Shift if needed) and a `python` on
PATH with `pypinyin`; without them the call reports `imeFallback` and still types the text via
unicode. Windows exposes no cross-process IME-state API, which is why the mode verifies the
result instead of trusting the mode.
- **Wheel**: split into 1–3-notch chunks with 25–85 ms gaps instead of one jump.

Pass `humanize: false` when a deterministic fast path is required (tests, bulk operations).
Measured here: 14 humanised characters took ~1.18 s; instant typing takes ~20 ms per character.

Because the Harness window takes the foreground back after each tool result, `computer_keyboard`
and `computer_mouse` accept `window` / `hwnd` and focus that window **inside the same call** as the
input. Without it, a "focus, then type" pair of separate calls can lose focus in between.

User mode cannot fake hardware: `SendInput` is the deepest documented API, and low-level hooks,
Raw Input consumers and anti-cheat can see the `LLMHF_INJECTED` flag. True hardware-grade input
needs a USB HID device (a Pico/Arduino/KMBox style adapter) or a kernel driver such as
Interception — both are outside this plugin, and kernel drivers carry real risk.

readme.section: Execution order: program first, recognition second, vision last
readme.text:
1. **Program control** — `computer_open` (shell launch) and `computer_window`
   (list / focus / minimize / maximize / restore / close / move) use Windows APIs directly.
2. **Program recognition** — `computer_uia` (UI Automation control tree: probe / tree / find /
   invoke / focus / setvalue) and `computer_find_text` / `computer_click_text` (built-in
   Windows OCR on a `PrintWindow` surface, so a covered window can still be read).
3. **Automatic routing** — `computer_act` probes one window and picks the channel itself:
   rich UIA tree → trigger the named control with `InvokePattern` / `ValuePattern` (no
   coordinates); thin tree or missing control → local OCR and a click. The result reports
   `channel: "uia" | "ocr"`.
4. **Vision fallback** — `computer_look` for non-text targets (icons, canvas, games) or an
   unclear plan.

readme.section: Browser pages: read them, never scan them
readme.text: A rendered page is data, not pixels. Three direct readers sit above OCR for that case:

readme.section: Browser pages: read them, never scan them
readme.text:
- **`computer_dom`** — a dependency-free CDP client. It connects to Edge/Chrome over
  `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/json/list` and speaks the DevTools WebSocket protocol directly, so
  `action: "text"` returns `document.body.innerText`, `action: "eval"` runs JavaScript and returns
  the value, `action: "click"` clicks a CSS selector, `action: "goto"` navigates. Measured here:
  text read **2 ms**, eval **6 ms**, launch (isolated profile) **577 ms**.
  Without a browser already started with `--remote-debugging-port`, `action: "launch"` starts
  Edge/Chrome with an isolated profile (default `<DSH_HOME>/browser-profile`; pass `profile` to
  keep it on another drive, e.g. `E:\dsh-browser`).
- **`computer_page_text`** — UI Automation `TextPattern` on the browser document, i.e. the
  accessibility tree text rather than the DOM. It works on Electron/Chromium windows too
  (measuring this Harness page: **7,218 characters** in one call, zero OCR). If the window exposes
  no `TextPattern`, it falls back to an OCR dump.
- **`computer_find_text` with an empty `text`** — dumps every recognized line of the window or
  region top-to-bottom (a chat pane, a canvas, a game HUD). Measured on a WeChat win

readme.section: Browser pages: read them, never scan them
readme.text:
Prefer HTTP (`web_fetch`) for public pages, CDP for logged-in/JS pages, `computer_page_text` for
Electron apps, and OCR only when there is no DOM at all.

Security note on CDP: `eval` runs arbitrary JavaScript in that browser profile. The debugging port
is bound to localhost, so keep it on the loopback interface and use a dedicated profile — do not
point it at a profile you also use for banking.

readme.section: Browser pages: read them, never scan them
readme.text:
Measured here: UI Automation is rich in Chromium/Electron windows (DeepSeek Harness
1040 named controls, Edge 576) and in native control apps (Calculator 49), but almost absent
in self-drawn apps (WeChat 1, classic Notepad 0). `computer_act` therefore invokes Calculator
buttons through UIA in ~1.3 s with no pixels involved, and falls back to OCR clicks for WeChat
in ~1.6 s.

readme.section: Browser pages: read them, never scan them
readme.text:
Everything uses documented Windows interfaces only: `SendInput`, GDI capture / `PrintWindow`,
window/process APIs, UI Automation, and `Windows.Media.Ocr`. No memory reads, injection, API
hooking, protocol emulation or credential handling — from the app's point of view it is a
normal user clicking and typing.

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| `computer_act` | One operation, automatic route: UIA Invoke/SetValue when the control tree is rich, else OCR + click. Reports which channel ran. |
| `computer_uia` | Inspect and drive the UI Automation tree: probe, tree, find, invoke, click, focus, setvalue. |
| `computer_open` | Open a program, file, folder or URL through the shell; returns the launched pid. |
| `computer_window` | List windows (title, pid, hwnd, rect, minimized); focus / minimize / maximize / restore / close / move one. |
| `computer_find_text` | OCR the screen or one window; returns matching lines with screen-pixel boxes and centers. With `scroll: true` it keeps scrolling and re-OCRing until the text appears (pure OCR, no vision). An empty `text` dumps every recognized line. |
| `computer_page_text` | Read a whole browser page (or any window with a UI Automation TextPattern) directly: UIA text first, local OCR dump as fallback. |
| `computer_dom` | CDP direct read: list page targets, read `innerText`/`outerHTML`, run JavaScript, click a selector, navigate, or launch a debuggable Edge/Chrome (isolated profile). |
| `computer_click_text` | OCR-locate text (optionally inside a wi

OCR details that make this reliable: tokens of one visual line are grouped into rows before
matching (Windows OCR splits `marker-180` into `marker`, `一`, `180`), dash-like glyphs and a
CJK `一` between ASCII characters normalize to `-`, CJK spacing is collapsed, minimised windows
are restored, and a `PrintWindow` capture that comes back blank is retried from the screen.

Web UI: a floating **电脑控制 / Computer Control** button in the bottom-right corner of the
Harness page opens a panel with a live preview, auto refresh, mouse controls and a
text/keys box. The panel calls the Host route `/dsh-computer-control/*`.

No OCR and no text extraction is involved: the frame is passed to the model as an
ordinary image content block, and the model itself interprets it natively (the `llm`
service exposes `ImageBlock`, `inputModalities: text | image` and a per-model
`imageRequestTarget`). `computer_look` therefore returns a model-written description of
the screen, with approximate coordinates, and the image object is unlinked before the
tool result is returned.

Cost note: a thinking model spends reasoning tokens on the look (a one-line answer took
~3k output tokens and ~20 s in testing). That nested call is not part of the Harness
turn accounting.

- `index.js` — Host half: the tools, `computer_look`, the prefix route on
  `ctx.webServer`, the frame worker, the transient-attachment lifecycle, cleanup, and the
  dependency-free CDP client.
- `scripts/screenshot-worker.ps1` — long-lived worker: one `Add-Type`/DPI setup, then one
  JSON line per capture on stdin/stdout, PNG returned as base64.
- `scripts/computer-control.ps1` — one-shot helper for mouse, keyboard, screen info,
  UI Automation, page text (`pagetext`) and explicit file/region captures (`SendInput` + `user32`).
- `client.js` — Client half: a `shell.overlay` entry with inline `zh`/`en` dictionaries
  registered through the Harness locale service.

Coordinates are physical screen pixels measured from the top-left of the primary monitor
(the helpers mark themselves per-monitor DPI aware).

- The plugin runs in the Harness Host process, so its tools are not constrained by the
  session's file sandbox. That is the point of the plugin — treat it as full local control.
- The route is served on the same origin as the Harness page and adds no authentication of
  its own; anything that can reach the local Harness port can call it.
- Windows only (`powershell.exe`, `user32.dll`, `System.Drawing`).
